title: ML Pipelines & Versioning
summary: Making a model's training run reproducible and safely automatable end to end.

slides.sectionTitle: The ML pipeline as a DAG
slides.subTitle: Ingest, features, train, validate, deploy
slides.markdown: Production ML rarely runs as one script — it's a **directed acyclic graph (DAG)** of steps: ingest raw data → compute features → train the model → validate against held-out data and quality gates → deploy. Structuring it as an explicit DAG (via tools like Airflow, Kubeflow Pipelines, or similar) rather than an ad-hoc notebook gives you three things a notebook can't: each step's inputs/outputs are tracked, failed steps can retry or alert without re-running everything upstream, and the whole pipeline can be triggered automatically (on a schedule, or by an upstream data-arrival event) instead of a person manually re-running cells. This structural shift — from notebook to DAG — is usually the first concrete step in taking a model from "a research result" to "a production system".

slides.subTitle: Logging parameters, metrics, and artifacts for every run
slides.markdown: Every training run should log, automatically: the hyperparameters used, the dataset version, the resulting metrics, and any output artifacts (the model file, a confusion matrix plot). Without this, a team ends up with the classic problem of a promising result buried in someone's terminal history that nobody can reproduce three weeks later — "I think I used a learning rate around 0.001, but I'm not sure" is a common, avoidable failure. Tools like MLflow or Weights & Biases make this close to free (a few lines of logging code per run) and turn "which run had the best F1 score, and exactly how was it configured" into a searchable question instead of an archaeology project.

slides.subTitle: Versioning and promoting models across environments
slides.markdown: A **model registry** is a central catalog of trained model versions, each tagged with its stage (staging, production, archived), its lineage (which experiment run produced it, on which data version), and often approval metadata (who signed off on promoting it). Promotion — moving a model from staging to production — becomes an explicit, auditable action rather than "someone copied a file to the prod server". This matters operationally too: if a newly-promoted model causes a regression, the registry makes rollback to the last known-good version a lookup-and-redeploy, not a scramble to remember which file was running last week.

slides.subTitle: Why code, data, and config all need pinning
slides.markdown: Reproducing a model requires more than pinning code — the **exact data** it was trained on matters just as much, and datasets change over time (new rows arrive, corrections are made, schemas evolve). **Data versioning** (tools like DVC, or dataset snapshots keyed by timestamp/hash) lets you say "this model was trained on data version `v42`" and actually retrieve that exact snapshot later, the same way git lets you retrieve exact code from any past commit. Without it, "reproduce last month's result" quietly becomes impossible the moment the underlying data table has been updated even once — the code is identical, but the data it now points to isn't.

slides.subTitle: Triggers that actually fire the DAG
slides.markdown: Once the pipeline is a well-defined DAG with tracked experiments and a registry, automating retraining becomes a matter of wiring up a **trigger**: a schedule (weekly), a drift alert (from monitoring, see [Model Monitoring & Drift](model-monitoring-drift)), or new labeled data crossing a volume threshold. The automated pipeline should still run the model through the same validation gates a human-triggered run would — a newly retrained model should never auto-promote to production without passing quality checks against a held-out set, since automation removes the human-in-the-loop review that would otherwise catch an obviously broken run.

slides.subTitle: Params, metrics, and artifacts in a few lines
slides.markdown:
A minimal experiment-tracking example with MLflow:

```python
import mlflow

with mlflow.start_run():
    mlflow.log_param("learning_rate", 0.001)
    mlflow.log_param("data_version", "v42")

    model = train(lr=0.001, data=load_data("v42"))
    f1 = evaluate(model)

    mlflow.log_metric("f1_score", f1)
    mlflow.log_artifact("confusion_matrix.png")
    mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, "model")
```

Every run is now queryable later: "show me all runs with `f1_score > 0.85`, sorted by `learning_rate`" is an actual query against tracked metadata, not a search through old notebooks.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: what triggers a retraining run
slides.markdown:
| Trigger | Catches | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Scheduled (weekly/monthly) | Gradual drift, predictable freshness | Retrains even when nothing has changed |
| New-data-volume threshold | Ensures enough new signal before retraining | Needs a labeling pipeline to keep pace |
| Drift alert | Reacts fast to a real distribution shift | Depends entirely on monitoring being accurate (see [Model Monitoring & Drift](model-monitoring-drift)) |

**How to decide:** a schedule alone wastes compute retraining on unchanged data, while drift-only triggers can miss slow gradual decay a threshold never crosses sharply — most mature pipelines combine a loose schedule as a floor with a drift alert as an early trigger.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: versioning the model but not the preprocessing code
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We version the trained model file and the raw data, so we're fully reproducible."

**Why it's wrong:** the preprocessing/feature-engineering code that transforms raw data into model inputs is itself a dependency — if that code changes (a bug fix to a normalization step, a new binning rule) without being versioned alongside the model, you can no longer reconstruct the exact inputs that model was trained on, even with the identical raw data and identical model file.

**Correct model:** version the full triplet — code (including preprocessing), data, and config — together, typically by pinning all three to a single experiment run ID rather than tracking them separately.

slides.subTitle: Testing a new model against real traffic without serving it
slides.markdown:
Before promoting a newly retrained model to production, a **shadow deployment** runs it alongside the current production model on real live traffic — the new model's predictions are logged and compared, but never actually shown to users or acted on. This catches a class of bug offline validation can miss: the new model behaves correctly on the held-out test set but reacts badly to some real-traffic pattern the test set didn't happen to include (a new user segment, a seasonal spike in a particular category).

Only after a shadow period shows the new model's predictions are at least as good on real traffic does it get promoted through the registry — turning "looked good in offline validation" into "also confirmed good on production-shaped data" before any user is affected.
